newsitem.title: SPAIN: No end to Spain strike seen after weekend talks.
newsitem.headline: No end to Spain strike seen after weekend talks.

text.p: Spain's government came under increasing pressure to end a truckers' strike with taxis and service stations threatening also to stop work on Monday.
The organisation leading the strike, Fedatrans, negotiated with the government throughout the weekend but no agreement was in sight as the stoppage entered its 12th day.
"The strike will not be called off," said Jose Luis Soldevilla, spokesman for the strikers. But negotiations were continuing late into the night and he acknowledged there was a "ray of light".
Soldevilla said the government, represented by Development Ministry Director General of Transport Fernando Cascales in the talks, was modifying its position.
Taxi drivers were threatening to join the strike on Monday, saying they want the same improvements in labour conditions and lower fuel prices the truckers are demanding.
Service stations also plan to strike, angered by government agreement to lower fuel prices to appease the truckers.
The strikers presented the government with a proposal on their key demands for lowering retirement age to 60 from 65, recognition of professional illnesses and curbing surging fuel prices.
Earlier they asked King Juan Carlos to mediate.
Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said on Sunday the government will take measures to avert economic paralysis if the strike continues.
The government warned on Friday the strike was causing grave damage to the economy and prices of fish and produce could rise sharply if it lasts.
Government sources said traffic was flowing freely and there were no more blockages at the borders with France and Portugal. Few incidents of violence were reported at the weekend.
The government has ordered security escorts for trucks after the strike jammed up border crossings, cut off roads, blocked ports and disrupted the supply of goods to northern Spain.
A number of domestic and foreign carmakers and other factories were forced to cut back or stop production due to a lack of raw materials.
Spanish media reported a number of service stations in the Santander region were closed on Sunday for lack of petrol.
Civil Guards were escorting convoys of trucks when drivers requested protection against possible retaliation from strikers parked along the hard shoulders of main roads in the north.
